rv.q: Joseph's writing captures the heat and colour of carnival, but also provides a more layered look at its history and political significance.
J'Ouvert is a rhapsodic piece of work, and a real joy to see.
J'Ouvert may be the closest we get to its exuberance this year.
This melange makes for some good moments in Yasmin Joseph’s play but the production as a whole feels diffuse and underpowered.
Joseph's text, lyrical, pulsing, woven with tunes and multi-roling, blends the past and present, the spiritual and the instant.

If one is simultaneously aware of an occasional untidiness, and a stylistic reach too far that at times stems the emotional flow, there's no denying the cumulative impact of an interval-free play fuelled, we're told, by 'anger and joy both [of which] live in your skin'.

cn.t: Joseph's vibrant debut captures Notting Hill Carnival's heat and exuberance while exploring its political significance, though critics are divided on its overall impact, with some finding it a beautifully rendered love letter and others less convinced.
